statement: Lecture 6 agenda: designing Gravatar, on-demand image optimization, tagging photos, designing a newly-unread message indicator; the notification-system design is already on YouTube.
detail: Board adds that 'Building a Notification System' is already put on YouTube ('watch it').
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Agenda - Designing Gravatar - On-demand Image Optimization - Tagging Photos - Designing Newly Unread Message Indicator

statement: When a request for an image URL hits a web server, the server reads the URL, reads the file at that path from its disk, and sends it as the response.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Once the request hits the server - reads the URL - reads the file from the server at the path - sends the response

statement: A static path such as /static/img/arpit.jpg maps onto the server's folder structure (site/static/img/arpit.jpg).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: https://arpitbhayani.me/static/img/arpit.jpg ... Folder structure site/ static/ img/ arpit.jpg logo.jpg js/ css/

statement: The browser renders the bytes returned for an img tag's URL as an image.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Bytes from the response are rendered as image

statement: The same endpoint can read the file from S3 instead of local disk: the handler takes the path from the URL, reads it from the S3 bucket and returns the bytes.
detail: Board also shows the call http://localhost:5000/raw/users/arpit.jpg with /users/arpit.jpg marked as request.path.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: @app.route('/raw/<path>') def raw_handler(path): raw_b = S3.read(path, BUCKET) return raw_b

statement: GitHub's og:image is an image generated dynamically for social sharing (the link preview card).
detail: Demonstrated on screen 00:16:30-00:26:30 with the DiceDB/dice repo: the og:image URL points at opengraph.githubassets.com and returns a 1200x600 PNG card with live repo stats.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: < GitHub og:image > dynamically gen[erated] image for social sharing

statement: Gravatar is a single embeddable URL for a user's profile picture, of the form https://gravatar.com/{hash(email)}.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Gravatar is your single embedable URL for profile picture https://gravatar.com/{hash(email)}

statement: The URL uses a hash of the email rather than the email itself for security, because the email is PII.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: → security PII

statement: If hash("arpit@gmail.com") = 0eafd172, embedding renders that user's current profile picture.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: if hash("arpit@gmail.com") = 0eafd172 Renders the current profile picture

statement: Gravatar requirements: a user can upload multiple pictures, can mark one as active, and the active one is returned in the response.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Requirements - user can upload multiple pictures - user can mark one as active - active one should be returned as part of the response

statement: Initial schema: users(id, email, hash) and photos(id, user_id, is_active).
detail: The hash column was struck through at first (00:35:45) and restored by 00:44:15.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: users id email hash photos id user_id is_active

statement: Fetching a user's photos joins photos with users on photos.user_id = users.id and filters by the user.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Select * from photos join on users on photos.user_id = users.id where user_id = ?

statement: Filtering with where HASH(email) = ? computes the hash at query time; the design instead stores a hash column and filters on users.hash.
detail: Audio (around 00:44) says the computed-hash where clause is very inefficient and needs a stored, indexed hash column.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: where HASH(email) = ? ... where users.hash = ?

statement: id, email and hash on users are all marked (starred) as indexed columns.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: * id * email * hash
flags: check: board only shows * before each column; that * means 'indexed' comes from audio around 00:44 ('creating an index on literally every single column')

statement: is_active on photos is a boolean.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: is_active : bool

statement: Marking a photo active takes two updates in one transaction: unset the user's currently active photo, then set the chosen photo active.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Tx update photos set is_active = False where user_id = ? ... update photos set is_active = true where id = ? Tx

statement: The unset update only touches the row that is currently active (where user_id = ? and is_active = True).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: update photos set is_active = False where user_id = ? and is_active = True

statement: The set update also checks ownership and current state: where id = ? and user_id = ? and is_active = false.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: where id = ? and user_id = ? and is_active = false

statement: The active photo is read with the users join plus and photos.is_active = True.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: where users.hash = ? and photos.is_active = True

statement: Better design: store active_photo_id on users, drop is_active from photos, and replace the two photo updates with one update users set active_photo_id = ? where hash = ?; reading becomes a lookup of photos by id.
detail: Board: is_active erased from photos (01:03:45), both update photos statements struck through (by 01:05:15); the third statement was first scrawled (01:02) and rewritten cleanly at 01:31. A scrawled 'Select * from photos where id = ?' follows the join queries.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: * active_photo_id ... update users set active_photo_id = ? where hash = ?

statement: Upload flow, prepare step: the user asks the photo upload service for a new upload; the service generates a random id and a signed URL for S3://gravatar-images/{user_id}/{random photo id} and sends the signed URL to the user.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: photo upload service generates signed URL for S3://gravatar-images/{user_id}/{random photo id}

statement: Upload step: the user uploads the photo directly to S3 using the signed URL.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Upload photo - user uploads photo to S3

statement: Sample rows: photos(7abe, 729, True); users(729, arpit@gmailcom, 0eafd172).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: 7abe 729 True ... 729 arpit@gmailcom 0eafd172

statement: Rendering the active photo at https://api.gravatar.com/photos/{hash}: get the hash from the URL, get the active photo id from the database, read the file from S3 at S3://gravatar-images/{user_id}/{photo id}, return the response.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: - get hash from the URL - get active photo id from the database - read the file from S3 - return the response

statement: To serve at https://gravatar.com/{hash}, configure gravatar.com as a CDN whose origin is api.gravatar.com/photos, so gravatar.com/hash maps to api.gravatar.com/photos/hash.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: let's use CDN to serve it Configure gravatar.com ——→ api.gravatar.com/photos

statement: Putting the CDN in front gives speed and scale of the CDN plus ease of use for the user (a short URL).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: We get, speed and scale of CDN & ease of use for user

statement: Architecture: on add/update the API writes MySQL and pushes an update event to a queue; a CDN Invalidation consumer invalidates the CDN path. On a CDN miss the CDN calls the API, which reads MySQL and S3.
detail: Diagram D-05. Red traces at 01:12:45 (update → queue → invalidation) and 01:13:15 (CDN → API → MySQL/S3).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: API update → queue → CDN Invalidation

statement: Possible optimization: denormalize the users table to avoid joins, e.g. store active_photo_id (or directly the active S3 key) on users.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Possible optimizations - You can denormalize the table to avoid Joins ... active_photo_id cdae ↑ active_S3_key

statement: On-demand image optimization: the original may be 1024x1024 but is rendered at 32x32; the client asks for a transformation in the URL query (e.g. ?w=32).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: 1024 x 1024 Render : 32x32 Transformation

statement: URL-driven image manipulation: the query parameter carries the transformation (e.g. https://edge.arpitbhayani.me/img/arpit.jpg?w=240), and CDNs offer this out of the box.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: URL driven image manipulations ... ?w=240 Query param contains the transformati[on] CDNs give this feature out of the box

statement: What the CDN does internally: read the URL; if it has the file, return it; if not, read the file from origin, transform it per the given transformations, cache it locally and return the response. The transform is the one extra step.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: - reads the URL - if it has the file, return - if not read the file from origin - transform as per ...

statement: On-demand image transformation is CPU intensive, cannot be made async, and needs large servers (in size and number).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: CPU intensive! Cannot be ASYNC large servers (size & numbers)

statement: ImageMagick is the library used for the transformations.
detail: Board spells it 'imagemagik' [sic]; audio says ImageMagick (01:25:27).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: "imagemagik"

statement: Store a tag's position relative to the image size, e.g. a point at (320,120) in a 720x720 image is stored as (320/720, 120/720).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Relative positioning location = ( 320/720 , 120/720 )

statement: Relative positions let the tag work on multiple devices and across on-demand transformations of the image.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Allows us to handle multiple devic[es] on-demand transformations at ea[ch]

statement: A tagged region can be stored as LTRB (left-top, right-bottom) or as x, y, w, h.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: LTRB / x,y,w,h

statement: Schema posts_tags(post_id, user_id, location).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: schema: posts_tags post_id | user_id | location

statement: Tagging interacts with other services: search, face detection, location, notification, and RBAC to check whether the user is authorized to tag.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Services to interact with: Search Face detection Location Notification RBAC [Authorized to tag?]

statement: Kafka is the key component for extensibility: publish a PHOTO_TAG event and let many consumers (search, notification, analytics, profile) react.

statement: Newly unread indicator: inform users about the presence of new messages, not the count of unread/unacked ones; the badge (e.g. 3) means 3 people you recently received messages from, even if there are hundreds of unread messages.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: We need to inform users about presence of new messages (not unread / unacked).

statement: Requirements: near-realtime, and update upon new messages received from a user.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Requirements: * near-realtime * update upon new messages received from user

statement: # new unreads = number of different people from whom a message was received and is unread.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: # new unreads = # different people from which message received and is unread

statement: Relational schema: user(id), user_activity(user_id, last_read_at), messages(msg, from, to, ts) with an index involving to (cut off on the board).
detail: Table first named 'lastread' (user, last_read) and 'msgs'. Green dots mark from, to, ts as the indexed columns; audio at 02:16:15 describes a composite index on from/to and timestamp.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: user id user_activity user_id last_read_at messages msg from to ts. index (t[o…]

statement: Crude approach: select count(uniq(from)) from messages where to = ? and ts > last_read_at on every load; it is correct but inefficient.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: CRUDE ... INEFFICIENT Select count(uniq(from)) from ... where to = ? & ts > last_read_at

statement: A pre-computed newly_unread_count per user was considered and struck; instead keep per user a set of unique senders and use its size.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: user_id: { newly_unread_count: 3 unique_users: set< > } ... user_id: unique_users set< >

statement: Delete the user's set when the user clicks the messages icon.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: delete set when user clicks "[icon]" icon

statement: Store it in a key-value store whose value is a set, e.g. Redis.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: K.value store value is set Redis

statement: The client calls getStatus to read the count and clear to reset it; both go through a service to Redis.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: getStatus clear ... Redis

statement: The messaging service knows over WebSockets whether a user is connected, so it can tell which messages were not delivered (or an online/offline service can).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Websockets know if a user is connected or not, we use thi[s] to find the undelivered messages

statement: The messaging service (WS connections, partitioned chat db) publishes ON_MSG_UNSENT events to a queue, and that event becomes the input to the unread system.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: ON_MSG_UNSENT Becomes the input to our system

statement: Each event contains src, dest and msg (e.g. src "A", dest "B"); per user we keep the unique senders, e.g. user_id : {u1, u2, u5}, B: {C, D}.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Each event would contain { src: "A" dest: "B" msg: "____" } ... UNIQUE USERS user_id : {u1, u2, u5}

statement: Read path: get_status and clean_status go to a Status check API backed by a Redis cluster.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: READ Path → get_status clean_status Status check API Redis Cluster

statement: Write path: ON_MSG_UNSENT events are consumed by status update workers that update the users' sets in Redis as each event arrives; the same stream also feeds the notification system.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: WRITE Path → Status update workers ... workers will update the users in Redis as it gets the event

statement: Writes can be batched at the workers when the queue is partitioned by recipient id.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: can batch here { if part = recv id
flags: check: second line read as '{ if part = recv id' (partition = receiver id); handwriting uncertain and the audio around 02:32-02:37 does not mention batching

statement: An auxiliary Redis sits in front of the main Redis cluster on the write path: workers record sender-recipient pairs (e.g. B_C : True, B_D : True) there and write to the main cluster only for a new pair; clearing status also deletes from the auxiliary store.
detail: Board shows only the pink Auxiliary Redis with lines from the workers and from the Status check API plus the B_C/B_D entries; the reasoning (n-1 redundant set writes, protect the brittle main DB) is in audio 02:33-02:40.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Auxiliary Redis ... B_C : True B_D : True
